subject: Private stack connection patterns: peering vs endpoint service vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Samuel Ortiz <s.ortiz@acme.com>
To: dylan_brooks@redwood.com
Cc: priya@acme.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: 2027-02-10T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Private deployment connection pattern / options

Hey Dylan + team,

Thanks for walking us through the private deployment options last week. We're trying to pick the right network pattern for Acme's initial integration with Redwood's private offering. Two quick constraints up front: our infra sits in a separate AWS account (same org) and we'll eventually have a small set of on-prem nodes (colocated analytics cluster) that need access during batch jobs.

High level ask: recommend one primary connectivity approach for the first pilot that balances security, observability, and predictable latency. Options we believe make sense:
- VPC peering (account-to-account)
- PrivateLink / endpoint service (interface endpoints)
- Site-to-site VPN to an Acme transit gateway (hybrid incl. on-prem)

I've attached a rough diagram and a small latency/cost spreadsheet (network-patterns-v1.png, latency-cost-estimates.xlsx). Specific questions:
1) Which approach gives us the best control over egress auditing and per-service access?
2) Any gotchas around cross-region or transitive routing (we expect a second region in 6 months)?
3) Bandwidth / throughput limits we should plan for on each pattern?

If easier, happy to do a 30-min technical call — we want to avoid rework once the pilot starts.

Thanks,
Samuel Ortiz
Senior Network Architect
Acme Analytics

Samuel — thanks for the clear summary and the attachments. Short answer: there isn't a one-size-fits-all, but we can pick a conservative default for the pilot and iterate.

Provisional plan:
- Pilot with PrivateLink (interface endpoint) for Redwood services per-account. Rationale: least blast-radius, simple ACL model, and we can tie access to IAM + endpoint policy.
- For on-prem batch jobs, complement with a short-lived S2S VPN (or use Direct Connect if you want dedicated bandwidth later).

That said, Karthik has a deeper checklist and cost/latency tradeoffs — I'll let him add the technical pros/cons. If Acme is open, we should do a 30-min call tomorrow to lock the pilot scope and list out routing/security checkpoints.

Action: Karthik, can you add a short matrix (latency, throughput, auditability, operational complexity) and any redlines we need to surface to procurement/security?

— Dylan Brooks

Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deployment connection pattern / options — technical matrix

Quick matrix below (summary, then recommendation):

1) VPC Peering (account-to-account)- Pros: Lowest added latency (L3, direct routing), straightforward for same-region, no additional endpoint services to manage.
- Cons: No transitive peering (peering does not route across other VPCs); cross-region peering has higher egress costs and operational overhead; peering requires updating route tables across each peer pair — becomes complex as number of VPCs grows.
- Throughput: effectively unlimited inside AWS but bound by instance ENI bandwidth; scale depends on instance types and path MTU.
- Auditability: standard VPC flow logs + AWS CloudTrail; harder to enforce per-service policies beyond Security Groups/NACLs.

2) PrivateLink / Interface Endpoint (AWS Endpoint Service)- Pros: Per-service access control (endpoint policies), supports cross-account securely without peering, hides service behind AWS-managed ENIs (better isolation), simpler client routing (no route table changes for consumers).
- Cons: Slightly higher latencies vs peering (extra hop to ENI) and per-GB data processing costs for endpoint. Requires you to publish an endpoint service or use AWS-provided endpoints.
- Throughput: nominally good for typical control-plane and API-style patterns; for very high sustained bulk throughput (heavy embedding calls, large data transfers) cost/latency can increase.
- Auditability: easy to enforce at service boundary and attach endpoint policies + CloudWatch metrics; good for least-privilege.

3) Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec)- Pros: Works for on-prem and multi-cloud; encrypted over public fabric; quick to stand up for pilots.
- Cons: Bandwidth caps and variable latency; long-lived tunnels require HA; operational complexity for routing (BGP) and failover. Not ideal for low-latency, high-throughput real-time inference.
- Throughput: typically limited by VPN appliance and AWS VPN throughput; Direct Connect recommended for sustained high bandwidth.

Recommendation for Acme pilot:
- Primary: PrivateLink for Redwood-facing service endpoints in Acme account. This gives per-service access control, clean audit boundaries, and minimal friction for Acme's security team.
- Complementary: Temporary S2S VPN to the Acme transit gateway for the on-prem cluster during batch windows; measure throughput and, if sustained, move to Direct Connect.
- Avoid: VPC peering as the primary path if you expect multi-VPC growth or cross-region access — peering becomes hard to manage and doesn't carry the same policy granularity as PrivateLink.

Operational notes / redlines:
- We'll need an endpoint policy template and a short-runbook for renewing/rotating endpoint IAM principals.
- Monitoring: enable VPC Flow Logs (to central log account), CloudWatch metrics on endpoints, and export VPN CloudWatch logs to Splunk/Datadog.
- DNS: PrivateLink requires DNS configuration (or use explicit endpoint IPs) — we'll include a stub playbook.
- Fallback: if PrivateLink shows unacceptable latency for large-batch inference, fallback to peering for that specific VPC pairing but restrict peering scope with strict SGs.

I attached a quick cost/latency sketch to the Drive link and column notes in the spreadsheet Samuel provided. Happy to go into any of these in the call.

Subject: Decision and pilot scope — Acme private connection

Thanks everyone for the rapid turnaround. Agreed on the staged approach — documenting final decisions here so security and procurement have a single source of truth.

Decision (pilot):
- Use PrivateLink (interface endpoints) as the primary connectivity pattern for Redwood services published into Acme's AWS account.
- Stand up a temporary Site-to-Site VPN to Acme's transit gateway for on-prem batch jobs. Evaluate bandwidth during the first two weeks; if sustained high throughput, migrate to Direct Connect.

Owners / deadlines:
- Karthik: endpoint policy + runbook, monitoring config, and DNS playbook — due 2027-02-14 EOD.
- Dylan: schedule the 30-min kickoff with Acme security + network, prep short checklist for Acme procurement — meeting scheduled for 2027-02-12 10:00 PT.
- Marissa: add procurement/contract redlines on data egress and support SLAs to the HubSpot deal (linked).

Samuel / Priya — please confirm that the proposed pilot scope works for Acme and whether you want Redwood to open the endpoint service or for Acme to request us as a provider. Once we have that, procurement can prepare the short mutual action plan.

Thanks,
Lauren Bishop
Director, Solutions & GTM Operations
Redwood Inference
